strengths: Addresses a clear gap: PET/CT is severely underrepresented in medical VLM literature relative to 2D and even 3D CT, and the paper is among the first to tackle mask-aware, lesion-level report generation for whole-body PET/CT.

Introduces PETAR-11K, a sizeable (11,356 lesion descriptions, 5,126 exams) dataset linking 3D PET/CT lesion segmentations to structured, referring-expression-style findings, along with a companion benchmark (PETAR-Bench) for standardized evaluation.

The architecture is reasonably well-motivated: shared 3D encoder for PET/CT, additive mask conditioning, and a focal-crop branch to counter the small-lesion/large-volume imbalance (lesions average <1% of volume), which the ablation shows is the single most impactful component.

Broad evaluation protocol spanning NLP n-gram metrics, semantic embedding metrics, and clinically-oriented LM metrics (RaTEScore, GREEN), complemented by two rounds of physician evaluation and a metric-to-human-judgment correlation study — a useful contribution in itself for the community given known unreliability of NLP metrics in radiology report generation.
Reasonably thorough ablation isolating the contribution of mask input, CT modality, and focal prompting, showing consistent, interpretable trends.
Comparison table and taxonomy (Table 1) clearly situate the work relative to prior 2D/3D and mask-aware medical VLMs.
weaknesses: The human evaluation is quite small: round 1 uses 100 pairs (physicians unspecified in number), and round 2 covers only 16 lesions from 8 patients across 5 raters — too limited to draw statistically robust conclusions about clinical utility, and no inter-rater agreement (e.g., Cohen's/Fleiss' kappa) is reported.

Dataset construction pipeline (SUVmax/slice-number sentence filtering, LLM ensemble extraction, iterative thresholding for mask generation) is not independently validated against manual segmentation or expert-annotated ground truth; no Dice/IoU or extraction precision/recall figures are given, leaving open the possibility of systematic label noise propagating into training and evaluation.

The dataset is restricted to sentences that explicitly mention both a slice number and SUVmax, which likely biases the corpus toward a specific reporting style and subset of lesions, and excludes normal/negative findings and lesions described without quantitative values — this narrows the scope of "automated reporting" claimed in the title, a point the Discussion itself partly concedes by noting full free-text report generation remains future work.

Baseline comparison fairness is unclear: some baselines are evaluated zero-shot while others (M3D-RAD, Reg2RG) are finetuned on the authors' data, and the paper states only the "best performing models in each category" were finetuned, without justifying or controlling for this asymmetry, which could inflate PETAR's relative gains.

The reported Spearman correlations between automated metrics and human scores are only moderate at best (GREEN 0.608, others much lower), yet the main results and SOTA claims rely heavily on these same metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, CIDEr, etc.), creating some tension between the paper's own findings and its evidentiary basis for the primary claims.

No statistical significance testing (e.g., confidence intervals, paired tests) is reported for the metric differences between PETAR and baselines, several of which (e.g., BLEU/METEOR vs. finetuned M3D-RAD) are numerically modest.

Reproducibility is limited: no explicit statement on public release of code, PETAR-11K, or PETAR-Bench (data is derived from a private clinical PET report corpus), and key implementation details (e.g., exact model sizes/backbones for all baselines, full hyperparameters) are deferred to supplementary material not included here.
Manuscript has multiple typographical errors (e.g., "experiemnts," "eopchs," "supplamnetary," "altneratively") suggesting incomplete proofreading.

The qualitative examples in Fig. 4 show PETAR making a localization/anatomic-subsite error relative to ground truth (e.g., sigmoid colon vs. proximal sigmoid colon mismatch details), which is not discussed as a limitation despite being presented as an illustrative example.

strengths: Introduces PETARSeg-11K, the first publicly described large-scale dataset linking lesion-level 3D PET/CT segmentation masks with free-text radiological findings (11,356 lesions, 5,126 exams), filling a clear gap relative to existing PET/CT resources (well documented in Table 1).

Proposes a technically reasonable architecture (PETAR-4B) that jointly encodes PET, CT, and lesion masks with a 3D focal-prompt mechanism specifically designed to preserve fine detail for lesions occupying <0.1% of volume, addressing a genuine limitation of prior global-encoding 3D medical VLMs.

Comprehensive evaluation combining eight automated metrics (n-gram, embedding-based, and LLM-based) with a human study involving five board-certified nuclear medicine physicians — reported as the first such study for PET report generation — adding credibility beyond automated scores alone.

Useful secondary contribution: correlating automated metrics with physician judgment (Table 4), which is a valuable finding for the community regarding which metrics (GREEN, RaTEScore) better reflect clinical quality versus n-gram metrics like BLEU.
Thorough ablation study isolating the contributions of mask input, CT modality, focal prompting, and TotalSegmentator pretraining, showing the focal prompt is the single largest contributor.
External validation on the autoPET dataset (distribution shift test) supports some generalizability of the approach beyond the internal cohort.
Clear discussion of limitations and a plausible future path toward a fully automated (mask-free) pipeline using existing lesion segmentation tools.
weaknesses: The human evaluation results are more equivocal than the narrative suggests: PETAR-4B scored consistently below human-written reports (3.7–3.9 vs 4.3–4.4) and was preferred in only 15/116 cases versus 47 cases where physicians preferred the human report; framing this as physicians preferring or tying the model ~60% of the time somewhat overstates the clinical parity claim.

The dataset's mask/text alignment pipeline depends on an automated LLM-based extraction and iterative-thresholding segmentation method from a separate prior work, with the reported 98% contour accuracy taken from that other paper rather than independently validated on this exact dataset/task; potential propagation of extraction or segmentation errors into both training and evaluation is not directly quantified here.

The model's dependence on lesion masks at inference time is a significant practical limitation for real-world automated reporting; the proposed fully automatic pipeline (using external lesion detectors) is discussed only as future work and not evaluated, so the paper's automated-reporting claims are partially aspirational.

Automated-metric comparisons across baselines are reported without variance/significance testing, and the paper's own analysis shows that even the best metric (GREEN) has only moderate correlation (ρ=0.59) with expert judgment, which somewhat undercuts the strength of claims like 'substantially outperforming all baselines' based primarily on these metrics.

The 2D baseline comparison protocol (3 orthogonal slices as a proxy for 3D context) may handicap 2D models relative to their normal operating conditions, making the 2D vs. 3D comparison less conclusive than presented.

Single-institution, single scanner-vendor (GE) data from 2010–2013 raises questions about generalizability to other scanners, protocols, and eras; combined with redacted institutional details, it's unclear whether/when the dataset will be made publicly available despite being described as such in the abstract.
Human evaluation is based on a relatively modest sample (116 internal pairs, 32 external cases) and 5 raters, limiting statistical power for subgroup or metric-correlation analyses.

The three-stage training procedure and dual global/focal encoding add architectural and training complexity; efficiency/latency trade-offs and sensitivity to hyperparameters are not deeply analyzed beyond the ablation table.

strengths: Introduces PETARSeg-11K, the first publicly described large-scale PET/CT dataset with lesion-level correspondence between 3D segmentation masks and free-text findings (11,356 lesions, 5,126 exams), filling a clear gap versus existing PET/CT datasets that lack either grounded masks or paired text findings (Table 1).

Proposes a well-motivated architecture (PETAR-4B) that jointly encodes PET, CT, and lesion masks with a 3D focal-prompt mechanism specifically designed to address the extreme small-lesion-in-large-volume problem (lesions <0.1% of volume), a distinct and clinically relevant technical challenge not addressed by prior mask-agnostic 3D medical VLMs (M3D, Merlin, CT2Rep) or organ-level mask methods (Reg2RG).

Comprehensive evaluation against a wide range of both 2D and 3D baselines, including finetuned versions for fair comparison, showing consistent and substantial improvements across n-gram, semantic, and LLM-based clinical metrics.

Includes a genuine human evaluation with five board-certified nuclear medicine physicians rating 116 real-vs-generated pairs plus an external out-of-distribution test on autoPET, which the authors credibly claim is the first such study for PET report generation — this substantially strengthens the clinical validity of the claims beyond automated metrics alone.

Useful secondary contribution correlating automated metrics with physician judgment (Table 4), providing practical guidance to the field on which metrics (e.g., GREEN, RaTEScore) better reflect clinical quality for this task.
Thorough ablation study isolating the contribution of mask input, CT modality, focal prompt, and TotalSegmentator pretraining, showing each component meaningfully contributes to performance.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility information in supplementary material (hyperparameters, prompts, data pipeline, scoring rubrics).
weaknesses: The dataset's lesion masks are automatically generated via an iterative thresholding/region-growing algorithm driven by LLM-extracted SUVmax/slice values rather than manually verified per-lesion in this work; the cited 98% contour accuracy comes from a different paper (Huemann et al.), and the accuracy of the LLM-based report parsing/normalization step itself is not independently validated in this manuscript, raising some concern about noise in the training/eval labels.

Human evaluation, while a strong addition, is relatively modest in scale (116 pairs from an internal set, 32 external cases) and physician-level agreement/inter-rater reliability statistics are not reported, making it harder to assess the robustness of the reported human scores.

PETAR-4B is only mildly preferred to real physician reports (preferred in 15/116, tied in 54/116, not preferred in 47/116) and scores measurably lower than human-written reports on all three rubrics (Table 5); the framing in the abstract/conclusion ("substantially outperforming baselines," "clinically useful") could be seen as slightly overstating clinical readiness relative to what the human study actually shows.

The method fundamentally requires an input lesion mask at inference time, meaning it does not perform lesion detection itself; the automated end-to-end pipeline (segmentation model + PETAR) is proposed only as future work and is not evaluated, so the practical, fully-automated utility of the system remains unproven.

Some baseline comparisons may not be fully apples-to-apples: 2D baselines are given only 3 representative slices while 3D and PETAR get full volumes plus explicit masks, and PETAR uniquely receives mask input that competing 3D baselines (except Reg2RG) do not use as designed, so part of the performance gap may reflect the mask-input advantage itself rather than purely architectural superiority; the ablation partially addresses this but a mask-informed baseline comparison beyond Reg2RG would strengthen the claim.

The dataset, despite being described as a key contribution, is drawn from a single institution/scanner vendor (GE Healthcare, single site, 2010-2013), which may limit generalizability of both the released dataset's diversity and the demonstrated model's applicability, despite reasonable external validation on autoPET.

Details on inter-annotator/LLM extraction pipeline errors (e.g., how often the ensemble LLMs made mistakes in extracting SUVmax/slice or disambiguating prior studies) and dataset release/licensing plan are not discussed, which affects reproducibility and trust in the pipeline's fidelity.

Numeric/quantitative details (lesion size, SUVmax) are explicitly acknowledged as frequently hallucinated by the model and were excluded from human evaluation scoring; while this is reasonably justified since these can be derived from masks, it does mean an important component of real PET reports is not being rigorously assessed for accuracy in the current evaluation.
